unit-sci-scales.source: Science 4, the measuring-practice sheets: rulers, graduated cylinders and thermometers

summary.text: The measuring-practice sheets are about reading real instruments: rulers to the nearest 0.1 cm (and converting to millimeters), graduated cylinders where you first have to work out what each unmarked line is worth, and thermometers — including reading between marks and below zero. The paper does the eye-training; this practices the REASONING behind every reading: figuring out the scale's interval, and placing a reading between two marks.

why.text: The Nature of Science test is Thursday 9/3, and scale-reading questions are free points once you have the one habit: before reading ANY instrument, work out what each line is worth. Every question here builds exactly that habit.

objectives.text: Work out what each unmarked line on a scale is worth, from the printed numbers and the line count.
Read a ruler to the nearest 0.1 cm, and convert between centimeters and millimeters.
Read a value that lands between two marked lines.
Read a thermometer below zero without flipping the direction.

parentNote.text: Built from the measuring-practice sheets and their answer key in the Quiz 1 Drive folder. Honest scope note: the sheets' actual pictures — where a bar ends, where a meniscus sits — can't be reproduced in the app without inventing them, so the paper stays the eye-practice and this unit drills the reasoning every reading depends on: the each-line-is-worth-what step, unit conversion, and between-the-marks readings, all with fresh numbers. Doing the paper sheets AND a round or two here covers both halves of the skill before the 9/3 test. The answer key checked out clean against the sheet — no misprints spotted.

nextUp.text: Do the paper sheets for the eye-practice, then a round here for the reasoning. The each-line-worth question is the whole game.

cards.term: The first question for ANY scale
cards.def:
**Before reading anything: what is each line worth?**
• Take two printed numbers, subtract them, and divide by the number of spaces between them.
• Marks at 40 and 50 with 5 spaces between → each line is worth 2.
cards.hint: Gap between printed numbers ÷ number of spaces.

cards.def:
**Each little millimeter line on a centimeter ruler is 0.1 cm.**
• A bar ending 3 small lines past the 7 reads 7.3 cm.
• "To the nearest 0.1 cm" just means: count the small lines.
cards.hint: Small lines = tenths of a centimeter.

cards.def:
**1 cm = 10 mm — slide the decimal one place.**
• 3.6 cm = 36 mm. 108 mm = 10.8 cm.
• The sheets ask for the SAME kind of length in both units, so the conversion is part of the reading.
cards.hint: cm to mm: number gets bigger ×10.

cards.def:
**Read the level against the nearest line — at eye level, at the BOTTOM of the curve.**
• Water in a cylinder curves up at the edges; the curve is called the meniscus, and you read its low point.
• First work out each line's worth; then count lines from the nearest printed number.
cards.hint: Eye level, bottom of the curve, nearest line.

cards.def:
**A level halfway between two lines reads as halfway between their values.**
• Between the 60 line and the 70 line, halfway up → 65.
• The sheets' small cylinders do this with tenths: halfway between 4.0 and 4.4 marks reads 4.2.
cards.hint: Split the difference between the two nearest lines.

cards.def:
**Below the 0 mark, numbers count UP as you go DOWN — but each line is still worth the same amount.**
• Two lines below zero on a 2-per-line scale is −4°C, not 4°C.
• Work out the line value the same way; only the sign changes.
cards.hint: Same line value, minus sign below zero.

cards.def:
**Two cylinders can both say 'mL' and be worth wildly different amounts per line.**
• The sheets jump from cylinders where a line is 0.2 mL to ones where a line is 25 mL.
• That's why the line-value step can never be skipped — the instrument doesn't announce it.
cards.hint: Never assume the line value carries over from the last one.

questions.q: A graduated cylinder has printed numbers at 20, 30 and 40 mL, with 5 spaces between each pair of printed numbers. What is each small line worth?
questions.hint: Gap between printed numbers, divided by the spaces between them.
steps: The gap between printed numbers is 30 − 20 = 10 mL.
That gap is cut into 5 spaces.
10 ÷ 5 = 2 mL per line.

ex.main: **2 mL.** Gap ÷ spaces, every time, before reading anything.
ex.tip: Count SPACES between the lines, not the lines themselves — off-by-one is the classic slip.

questions.q: A graduated cylinder's small lines are worth 2 mL each. The water level sits exactly 3 lines above the 30 mL mark. What is the volume?
questions.hint: Start at the printed number and add per line.
steps: Each line is worth 2 mL.
3 lines above 30 adds 3 × 2 = 6 mL.

ex.tip: 33 mL is the trap answer — that's counting each line as 1. The line value question always comes first.

questions.q: A bar on a centimeter ruler ends 7 small lines past the 4 cm mark. What is its length to the nearest 0.1 cm?
questions.hint: Each small line on a cm ruler is 0.1 cm.
steps: Small lines on a centimeter ruler mark tenths: 0.1 cm each.
7 small lines past the 4 is 4 + 0.7.
Length: 4.7 cm.

ex.main: **4.7 cm.** Whole centimeters from the big number, tenths from the small lines.
ex.tip: Always check the bar starts at 0 — a bar running from 2 to 6.7 is 4.7 cm too, but you'd have to subtract.

questions.q: A bar measures exactly 4.7 cm. What is its length in millimeters?
steps: 1 cm = 10 mm, so multiply centimeters by 10.

ex.main: **47 mm.** Same length, smaller unit, bigger number — the decimal slides one place right.
ex.tip: The sheets ask some bars in cm and some in mm on purpose — the conversion is part of the tested skill.

questions.q: A small graduated cylinder is printed every 1 mL, with 5 spaces between printed numbers. The water's meniscus bottoms out 1 line above the 6 mL mark. What is the volume?
questions.hint: First: what's each line worth on a 1-mL-per-number scale with 5 spaces?
steps: The gap between printed numbers is 1 mL, cut into 5 spaces: each line is 1 ÷ 5 = 0.2 mL.
1 line above 6 adds 0.2 mL.
Reading: 6.2 mL — taken at the bottom of the meniscus curve.

ex.main: **6.2 mL.** Small cylinders make the line value a fraction — exactly like the sheet's 4.2 and 7.6 mL cylinders.
ex.tip: 6.1 assumes tenths per line; 6.5 assumes halves. The 5-space count is what settles it: 0.2 each.

questions.q: Why is a graduated cylinder read at the BOTTOM of the water's curve, at eye level?
opts: Water climbs the walls a little, so the low point is the true level
The bottom of the curve is easier to see from above
Reading the top of the curve is also correct
Cylinders are only accurate when half full
questions.hint: The curve is called the meniscus — why does it exist?
steps: Water sticks to the cylinder's walls (adhesion), so its surface curves upward at the edges.
That curve — the meniscus — makes the edges read falsely high.
The low point in the middle is the actual water level, and eye level keeps the angle from distorting it.

ex.main: **The curve's low point is the true level.** The edges are water climbing the walls, not extra volume.
ex.tip: Eye level matters as much as the meniscus — reading from above tilts the whole scale.

questions.q: A thermometer is printed every 10°C with 5 spaces between printed numbers. The liquid tops out 2 lines above the 30°C mark. What is the temperature?
questions.hint: Work out the line value before counting.
steps: Gap of 10°C over 5 spaces → each line is 2°C.
2 lines above 30 adds 2 × 2 = 4°C.
Temperature: 34°C.

ex.main: **34°C.** Same two-step as every scale: line value first, then count from the nearest printed number.
ex.tip: 32°C is the count-lines-as-ones trap again — it follows you from instrument to instrument.

questions.q: A thermometer's lines are worth 2°C each. The liquid sits 3 lines BELOW the 0°C mark. What is the temperature?
questions.hint: Below zero, the lines are still worth 2°C each — only the sign changes.
steps: Each line is still worth 2°C below zero.
3 lines below 0 is 3 × 2 = 6 degrees below.
Below zero means negative: −6°C.

ex.main: **−6°C.** The scale keeps its line value across zero; the direction of counting is what flips.
ex.tip: Cold-weather readings are where a rushed reading drops the minus sign — say 'below zero' out loud as you write it.

questions.q: A big cylinder is printed at 400, 500, 600 and 700 mL with 4 spaces between printed numbers. The level sits 1 line above 600. A tiny cylinder is printed every 1 mL with 5 spaces. Which statement is right?
opts: It reads 625 mL — each line is worth 25 mL, far more than the tiny one's
Both cylinders' lines are worth the same, since both measure mL
questions.hint: Work out BOTH line values — 100 ÷ 4 and 1 ÷ 5.
steps: Big cylinder: gap 100 mL over 4 spaces → 25 mL per line. 1 line above 600 = 625 mL.
Tiny cylinder: gap 1 mL over 5 spaces → 0.2 mL per line.
Same unit printed on both, but each line is worth over 100 times more on the big one — which is why the line-value step can never be skipped.

ex.main: **625 mL — and the two instruments' lines differ by over 100×.** The sheet jumps between exactly these kinds of cylinders back to back.
ex.tip: The unit label (mL) tells you WHAT is measured, never HOW MUCH each line is worth.

questions.q: A student reads a cylinder by counting 4 lines up from the 50 mL mark and writes "54 mL." The scale is printed every 25 mL with 5 spaces between numbers. What went wrong?
opts: Each line is worth 5 mL, not 1 — the reading is 70 mL
She should have read the top of the meniscus
She counted from the wrong end — it's 46 mL
questions.hint: 25 mL split into 5 spaces makes each line worth how much?
steps: The gap between printed numbers is 25 mL, over 5 spaces → each line is 5 mL.
4 lines above 50 adds 4 × 5 = 20 mL.
The right reading is 70 mL — she skipped the line-value step and defaulted to 1 per line.

ex.main: **Each line was worth 5 mL, so the reading is 70 mL.** Spotting the skipped step in someone else's work is the surest sign you own the skill.
ex.tip: If a reading was this easy to get wrong silently, that's the test question they'll ask — expect a find-the-mistake item.
